submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole is a retrospective detector for the word material of technical, scientific and reference prose: it fires on the substantive, mostly Greco-Latin vocabulary of laboratory, clinical, physical-science, mathematical and bibliographic text (aliquot, phosphate, buffer, serum, plasma, protein, antibody, supernatant, immunoblot, reagent, centrifuged, maintained, constant, minutes, process, XRD, FTIR, pp.) and on the subword fragments such words split into (plasm, ot in Monotone/Nicotiana, ogly+cans, roph, iter, rom, ror, inc, com), and on LaTeX, code-identifier and mojibake tokens (frac, mathbb, sqrt, href, std, '�'). It sits at the GELU floor (0.000 of its 2.69 maximum) on function words and on ordinary everyday vocabulary (the, of, was, dog, house, water, chair, bread, money, very, happy, brother, shop) whatever the sentence is about, and the register of the preceding text gates it: the identical sentence 'The plasma was collected from each patient.' puts 'plasma' at 0.25 of max after three sentences of laboratory prose but at exactly 0.000 after three sentences of story or news prose, and ' measured' is 0.35 of max after 'We' but 0.00 after 'She'.

rival_explanations: Narrower, biomedical-only: the pole is a wet-lab vocabulary detector (a fitted key tops out at IGF, immunoblot, RPMI, ChIP, phospho-, -ogly, RNase, supernatant), so it should sit near its floor on the scan's physics, mathematics, bibliography and software examples (XRD, Monotone, Tristram, pp., MatrixDecomposer) and on new technical text from those fields.

Broader, unfamiliarity: the pole fires on any token that is rare or out of distribution rather than on technical register, so it should fire as strongly on rare everyday words and rare proper nouns (wheelbarrow, cauliflower, chromatography, Smith, Jones) and its strength should track token rarity rather than domain.

Word-internal position: the pole fires on subword fragments (tokens without a leading space) wherever they occur, so it should be as active on the second piece of an everyday long word (the 'ing' of walking, the 'er' of garden) as on 'plasm', and the plasm/plasma spelling change alone should explain its peaks.

В этом ярком свекольном салате есть свежие овощи и один вареный, что создает интересную вкусовую и текстурную комбинацию.
Тертый салат — комфортное блюдо, которое легко и быстро готовить, удобно есть и подавать, особенно когда в составе имеются сырые твердые овощи, как в этом рецепте с кулинарного канала Cuisine Marocaine.
К овощам в салате добавляются яйца. Автор рецепта советует варить их в воде с небольшим количеством уксуса. Считается, что кислота предотвращает вытекание белка и облегчает чистку вареного яйца.
Узнайте: Как быстро почистить вареные яйца
Яйца можно натереть и вмешать в салат или разрезать в четыре части и выложить вокруг блюда.
Попробуйте также быстрый салат из сырой свеклы.
Картошку отварите в мундире. Яйца отварите вкрутую.
Сырую очищенную свеклу натрите на крупной терке. Очистите огурец и также крупно натрите, отожмите сок. Добавьте огурец к свекле. Натрите к овощам очищенный картофель.
Лук нашинкуйте, петрушку мелко нарежьте, закиньте к овощам.
Приправьте салат солью и перцем, полейте растительным маслом по вкусу. Сверху натрите вареные яйца и перемешайте. Добавьте майонез и украсьте петрушкой.
Свекла — вкусный и полезный овощ, один из главных корнеплодов в нашем рационе. Он неприхотлив и хорошо сохраняется, но есть некоторые нюансы. Узнайте, как правильно хранить свеклу, чтобы она не теряла свои ценные свойства.

He appeared almost immediately, an inquiring look on his face.

"How can I serve you, Miss Cavendish?" he said, deferentially.

"By permitting us to go out for some air--these rooms were not designed, apparently, for permanent residence."

"It can be arranged," he answered. "When do you wish to go?"

"At once!"

"Very good!" he said. "You will have no objection to being attended, to make sure you don't stray off too far, you know?"

"None whatever, if the attendant remains at a reasonable distance."

He bowed and stood aside.

"You may come," he said.

"Is the locality familiar?" Elaine asked, when they were some distance from the house.

Davila shook her head. "It is south of Hampton, I think, but I can't give any reason for my impression. The car was running very rapidly; we were, I reckon, almost two hours on the way, but we can't be more than fifty miles away."

"If they came direct--but if they circled, we could be much less," Elaine observed.

"It's a pity we didn't think to drop something from the car to inform our friends which way to look for us."

"I did," said Elaine. "I tossed out a handkerchief and a glove a short distance from Hampton--just as I struck that fellow. The difficulty is, there isn't any assurance we kept to that road. Like as not, we started north and ended east or south of town. What is this house, a fishing club?"

"I rather think so. There is a small wharf, and a board-walk down to the Bay, and the house itself is one story and spread-out, so to speak."

"Likely it's a summer club-house, which these men have either rented or preempted for our prison."

"The country around here is surely deserted!" said Davila.

"Hence, a proper choice for our temporary residence."

"I can't understand the care they are taking of us--the deference with which we are treated, the food that is given us."

"Parmenter's treasure, and the prize they think they're playing for, has much to do with it. We are of considerable value, according to their idea."

After a while, they went back to the house. The two men, who had remained out of hearing, but near enough to prevent any attempt to escape, having seen them safely within, disappeared. As they passed through the hall they encountered the chief. He stepped aside.

"You enjoyed your walk, I trust?" he said.

Davila nodded curtly. Elaine stopped.

"I feel sorry for you!" she said, smiling.

"You are very kind," he replied. "But why?"

"You are incurring considerable expense for nothing."

He grinned. "It is a very great pleasure, I assure you."

"You are asking the impossible," she went on. "Mr. Croyden told you the simple truth. He _didn't_ find the Parmenter jewels."

The man's face showed his surprise, but he only shrugged his shoulders expressively, and made no reply.

"I know you do not believe it--yet it's a fact, nevertheless. Mr. Croyden couldn't pay your demands, if he wished. Of course, we enjoy the experience, but, as I said, it's a trifle expensive for you."

Significance of Irony
The irony in a text is a literary device that is used in the illustration of a situation whereby the end outcome is contrary to what was expected by the audience. This is one of the most common devices that are used in stories and plays and plays a significant role in the script. Usually, the authors ensure that some of the characters in the book depict this aspect. One of the most important roles that irony plays is the fact that it initiates humor among the audience. This breaks the boredom among the audience and increases their concentration, as they are anxious about the end. The irony in play is important because it creates anxiety among the readers as they are eager to find out the next step or situation only to find out that it is very different from what they expected.
On the other hand, the relevance of the text is critical especially to the targeted audience. Literary devices are often used to bring in connection in a play or an individual storyline. One example of irony in a text is the dramatic irony that is often employed by many authors in their work. It ensures that knowledge is passed through the audience. The audience tends to be keen on cases or scenes of drama in a text. This aspect of omniscience cannot be experienced in our lives, but we can enjoy it in literature. Also, the audience is expected to evaluate the book regarding the devices that are used and the manner in which the different characters conduct themselves. This implies that the public can judge a character and provide alternative ways of appreciating the characters actions and personality. This is evident, as we have seen in some plays where the characters who are put in scenes of dramatic irony are often the main characters and best and at times with bad personalities according to the readers.
Literature is not only about knowledge but at times it is considered as fun, and in this way, it can be used as a source of enjoyment especially when we watch the plays. In this case, irony brings a sense of humor and fun in play thus engaging the audience throughout. Irony is used to distinguish between right and wrong. In many cases, we tend to have a perception of a particular outcome in a play or novel. We tend to understand this differences depending on the manner in which characters play their role. Also, another significant role that irony plays is to ensure that it provides a reflection of how we live in the society. This has been applied in true stories where the author tries to incorporate real life situations that the social experiences. Irony mainly revolves around family or even friends where close individual betrays others contrary to the audience’s expectation.

readings.explanation: The pole is a retrospective detector for the word material of technical, scientific and reference prose: it fires on the substantive, mostly Greco-Latin vocabulary of laboratory, clinical, physical-science, mathematical and bibliographic text (aliquot, phosphate, buffer, serum, plasma, protein, antibody, supernatant, immunoblot, reagent, centrifuged, maintained, constant, minutes, process, XRD, FTIR, pp.) and on the subword fragments such words split into (plasm, ot in Monotone/Nicotiana, ogly+cans, roph, iter, rom, ror, inc, com), and on LaTeX, code-identifier and mojibake tokens (frac, mathbb, sqrt, href, std, '�'). It sits at the GELU floor (0.000 of its 2.69 maximum) on function words and on ordinary everyday vocabulary (the, of, was, dog, house, water, chair, bread, money, very, happy, brother, shop) whatever the sentence is about, and the register of the preceding text gates it: the identical sentence 'The plasma was collected from each patient.' puts 'plasma' at 0.25 of max after three sentences of laboratory prose but at exactly 0.000 after three sentences of story or news prose, and ' measured' is 0.35 of max after 'We' but 0.00 after 'She'.

Narrower, biomedical-only: the pole is a wet-lab vocabulary detector (a fitted key tops out at IGF, immunoblot, RPMI, ChIP, phospho-, -ogly, RNase, supernatant), so it should sit near its floor on the scan's physics, mathematics, bibliography and software examples (XRD, Monotone, Tristram, pp., MatrixDecomposer) and on new technical text from those fields.

Broader, unfamiliarity: the pole fires on any token that is rare or out of distribution rather than on technical register, so it should fire as strongly on rare everyday words and rare proper nouns (wheelbarrow, cauliflower, chromatography, Smith, Jones) and its strength should track token rarity rather than domain.

Word-internal position: the pole fires on subword fragments (tokens without a leading space) wherever they occur, so it should be as active on the second piece of an everyday long word (the 'ing' of walking, the 'er' of garden) as on 'plasm', and the plasm/plasma spelling change alone should explain its peaks.
